content_of_post_to_comment: This post correctly identifies the bureaucratic bloat affecting universities. Why has it happened in so many different countries? I have argued (in a report to the Australian Parliament) that it partly reflects managerial capture. Higher education is an industry with relatively little ecological pressure in the form of competition. Universities’ business relies on a steady flow of students, driven in large part by reputational rankings that take years to change. This contrasts with many other industries, where management faces immediate pressure in the event of poor performance. The consequences of poor managerial choices can take years to eventuate in universities, and may only become noticeable after the tenure of the managers responsible. Low ecological pressure gives universities some degree of market power, creating rents, while the typical absence of tight control by stakeholders (there are no shareholders’ meetings holding university management accountable) creates scope for managerial capture. These rents can then be used to fund managers’ preferences in the form of high salaries, large numbers of staff (“empire building”), and prestigious real-estate projects. The large flow of funds into universities in countries such as the US, UK and Australia, where students pay substantial amounts for their education, has given management the financial means to build a bloated army of administrative staff. This has often come with a reduction in academic autonomy and a gradual erosion of the academic character of these institutions.
comment: A missing piece may be the feedback loop: administrative growth can initially solve real coordination problems, but without competitive pressure those solutions become permanent structures. The challenge is distinguishing necessary complexity from self-sustaining bureaucracy.
